explanation: The heart was thought to hold the mind and was weighed in the afterlife. The brain was usually thrown away, while the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines were often stored in canopic jars.

claims.text: Egyptian embalmers usually left the heart inside the body.
The brain was usually removed and discarded, and the liver and lungs were removed and preserved separately.
Ancient Egyptians believed the heart held the mind and would be weighed in judgement in the afterlife.
The liver, lungs, stomach and intestines were often preserved in canopic jars.

evidence.restatement: Egyptian embalmers usually left the heart in the body.
They drew out and discarded the brain, and removed the liver and lungs to preserve them separately.
The heart was seen as the seat of mind and conscience and was weighed at the judgement of the dead.
The liver, lungs, stomach and intestines were often stored in canopic jars.
Embalmers normally left the heart in the chest.

claimResults.note: Rival test: the brain was drawn out through the nose and discarded; liver and lungs were removed. 'Usually' is the right hedge, since viscera were later returned to the body in packets but the heart was never taken out.

evidence.restatement: The brain was drawn out and thrown away; the liver and lungs were removed and treated separately.
The Egyptians placed the mind in the heart, and the Book of the Dead shows it weighed against the feather of Ma'at.
Canopic jars held the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines.

editor.reason: Both checks pass on certain knowledge, and every claim is standard risk. The distractors are the organs embalmers removed, all definitely wrong, and 'usually' covers the later habit of returning wrapped viscera to the body.

stem: When making a mummy, which organ did ancient Egyptian embalmers usually leave in the body?
